claim: Chronic lung diseases present tremendous health burdens attributed to dysfunctional alveolar repair.
source: Chronic lung diseases present tremendous health burdens attributed to dysfunctional alveolar repair (Barnes et al., 2015; Lozano et al., 2012; Spella et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Barnes et al., 2015; Lozano et al., 2012; Spella et al., 2017).

claim: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is the leading cancer killer worldwide.
source: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), the leading cancer killer worldwide, is mainly caused by chemical carcinogens of tobacco smoke that induce mutations of the Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homologue (KRAS) in yet unidentified pulmonary cells (Torre et al., 2015; Forbes et al., 2011; Hecht, 1999; Campbell et al., 2016; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Torre et al., 2015).

claim: Lung adenocarcinoma is mainly caused by chemical carcinogens of tobacco smoke that induce mutations of KRAS in yet unidentified pulmonary cells.
source: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), the leading cancer killer worldwide, is mainly caused by chemical carcinogens of tobacco smoke that induce mutations of the Kirsten rat sarcoma viral oncogene homologue (KRAS) in yet unidentified pulmonary cells (Torre et al., 2015; Forbes et al., 2011; Hecht, 1999; Campbell et al., 2016; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Forbes et al., 2011; Hecht, 1999; Campbell et al., 2016; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014).

claim: Epithelial developmental pathways are intimately related with oncogenic signaling to jointly regulate stemness and drug resistance.
source: The discovery of the cellular lineages and the transcriptional programs that underlie lung regeneration and carcinogenesis is extremely important, since epithelial developmental pathways are intimately related with oncogenic signaling to jointly regulate stemness and drug resistance (Barbie et al., 2009; Seguin et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Barbie et al., 2009; Seguin et al., 2014).

claim: Lineage-specific genes encoding epithelial proteins that support the physiological functions of the lungs suffer non-coding insertions and deletions in LUAD.
source: To this end, lineage-specific genes encoding epithelial proteins that support the physiological functions of the lungs were recently shown to suffer non-coding insertions and deletions in LUAD, lending further support to the longstanding notion that epithelial cells that express lung-restricted proteins are the cellular sources of LUAD (Imielinski et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Imielinski et al., 2017).

claim: Epithelial cells that express lung-restricted proteins are the cellular sources of LUAD.
source: To this end, lineage-specific genes encoding epithelial proteins that support the physiological functions of the lungs were recently shown to suffer non-coding insertions and deletions in LUAD, lending further support to the longstanding notion that epithelial cells that express lung-restricted proteins are the cellular sources of LUAD (Imielinski et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to published literature (Imielinski et al., 2017) and described as a longstanding notion.

claim: Previous pulmonary lineage tracing studies incriminated both airway and alveolar cells as progenitors of newly formed alveoli and/or LUAD in adult mice.
source: Previous pulmonary lineage tracing studies that utilized noxious insults and ectopic expression of oncogenes in the respiratory epithelium incriminated both airway and alveolar cells as progenitors of newly formed alveoli and/or LUAD in adult mice (Zuo et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2005; Cho et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2012; Sutherland et al., 2014; Mainardi et al., 2014; Desai et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Zuo et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2005; Cho et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2012; Sutherland et al., 2014; Mainardi et al., 2014; Desai et al., 2014).

claim: Airway epithelial cells (AEC) line the bronchi and include ciliated, basal, goblet, and Clara or club cells.
source: To this end, airway epithelial cells (AEC) line the bronchi and include ciliated, basal, goblet, and Clara or club cells; alveolar type II cells (ATII) and alveolar macrophages (AMΦ) are distributed across the distal lung parenchyma; and bronchoalveolar stem cells (BASC) with dual AEC/ATII properties are located at the bronchoalveolar junctions.
evidence: Described as established knowledge in the field, with references to markers in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and extensively studied in Desai et al. (2014) and Treutlein et al. (2014).

claim: Alveolar type II cells (ATII) and alveolar macrophages (AMΦ) are distributed across the distal lung parenchyma.
source: To this end, airway epithelial cells (AEC) line the bronchi and include ciliated, basal, goblet, and Clara or club cells; alveolar type II cells (ATII) and alveolar macrophages (AMΦ) are distributed across the distal lung parenchyma; and bronchoalveolar stem cells (BASC) with dual AEC/ATII properties are located at the bronchoalveolar junctions.
evidence: Described as established knowledge in the field, with references to markers in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and extensively studied in Desai et al. (2014) and Treutlein et al. (2014).

claim: Bronchoalveolar stem cells (BASC) with dual AEC/ATII properties are located at the bronchoalveolar junctions.
source: To this end, airway epithelial cells (AEC) line the bronchi and include ciliated, basal, goblet, and Clara or club cells; alveolar type II cells (ATII) and alveolar macrophages (AMΦ) are distributed across the distal lung parenchyma; and bronchoalveolar stem cells (BASC) with dual AEC/ATII properties are located at the bronchoalveolar junctions.
evidence: Described as established knowledge in the field, with references to markers in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and extensively studied in Desai et al. (2014) and Treutlein et al. (2014).

claim: Existing mouse models for lineage tracing feature incomplete and/or promiscuous lung cell labeling.
source: However, existing mouse models for lineage tracing feature incomplete and/or promiscuous lung cell labeling, that is cellular markings fail to identify all cells of a target lineage (false negative marking) or wrongfully identify other cells outside of the target lineage (false positive marking) (Zuo et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2005; Cho et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2012; Sutherland et al., 2014; Mainardi et al., 2014; Desai et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Zuo et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2005; Cho et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2012; Sutherland et al., 2014; Mainardi et al., 2014; Desai et al., 2014).

claim: All studies that attempted to address the cellular origins of LUAD to date employed overexpression of oncogenes such as KRASG12D in the lungs.
source: In addition, all studies that attempted to address the cellular origins of LUAD to date employed overexpression of oncogenes such as KRASG12D in the lungs, to conclude that ATII cells or BASC are the most probable culprits of the disease (Kim et al., 2005; Cho et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2012; Sutherland et al., 2014; Mainardi et al., 2014; Desai et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Kim et al., 2005; Cho et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2012; Sutherland et al., 2014; Mainardi et al., 2014; Desai et al., 2014).

claim: Previous studies concluded that ATII cells or BASC are the most probable culprits of LUAD.
source: In addition, all studies that attempted to address the cellular origins of LUAD to date employed overexpression of oncogenes such as KRASG12D in the lungs, to conclude that ATII cells or BASC are the most probable culprits of the disease (Kim et al., 2005; Cho et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2012; Sutherland et al., 2014; Mainardi et al., 2014; Desai et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Kim et al., 2005; Cho et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2012; Sutherland et al., 2014; Mainardi et al., 2014; Desai et al., 2014).

claim: Oncogenic KRASG12D-driven mouse lung tumors do not imitate the mutational landscape of human LUAD as closely as tobacco carcinogen-induced LUAD do.
source: However, it was recently shown that oncogenic KRASG12D-driven mouse lung tumors do not imitate the mutational landscape of human LUAD as closely as tobacco carcinogen-induced LUAD do (Campbell et al., 2016; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014; Westcott et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to published literature (Campbell et al., 2016; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2014; Westcott et al., 2015).

claim: GFP;CCSP.CRE mice show permanent genetic GFP-labeling of all airway cells.
source: This approach labeled permanently all AEC of GFP;CCSP.CRE mice, some AEC and all ATII of GFP;SFTPC.CRE mice, some ATII and all AMΦ of GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice, and various other cells in the remaining intercrosses (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplements 3–5, and Figure 1—figure supplement 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplements 3–5.

claim: GFP;SFTPC.CRE mice show permanent genetic GFP-labeling of some AEC and all ATII.
source: This approach labeled permanently all AEC of GFP;CCSP.CRE mice, some AEC and all ATII of GFP;SFTPC.CRE mice, some ATII and all AMΦ of GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice, and various other cells in the remaining intercrosses (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplements 3–5, and Figure 1—figure supplement 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplements 3–5.

claim: GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice show permanent genetic GFP-labeling of some ATII and all AMΦ.
source: This approach labeled permanently all AEC of GFP;CCSP.CRE mice, some AEC and all ATII of GFP;SFTPC.CRE mice, some ATII and all AMΦ of GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice, and various other cells in the remaining intercrosses (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplements 3–5, and Figure 1—figure supplement 5—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplements 3–5.

claim: Genetic GFP-labeling in GFP;CCSP.CRE mice marked all airway epithelial cells including club and ciliated cells.
source: Co-localization of GFP-labeling with lineage protein markers (listed in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) revealed that genetic GFP-labeling in GFP;CCSP.CRE mice marked all airway epithelial cells including club and ciliated cells, in GFP;SFTPC.CRE mice most airway and all alveolar epithelial type II cells, and in GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice some alveolar epithelial type II cells and all alveolar macrophages (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 6–8, Figure 1—figure supplement 7—source data 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 8—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplements 6–8.

claim: GFP;SFTPC.CRE mice show genetic GFP-labeling in most airway and all alveolar epithelial type II cells.
source: Co-localization of GFP-labeling with lineage protein markers (listed in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) revealed that genetic GFP-labeling in GFP;CCSP.CRE mice marked all airway epithelial cells including club and ciliated cells, in GFP;SFTPC.CRE mice most airway and all alveolar epithelial type II cells, and in GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice some alveolar epithelial type II cells and all alveolar macrophages (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 6–8, Figure 1—figure supplement 7—source data 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 8—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplements 6–8.

claim: GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice show genetic GFP-labeling in some alveolar epithelial type II cells and all alveolar macrophages.
source: Co-localization of GFP-labeling with lineage protein markers (listed in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) revealed that genetic GFP-labeling in GFP;CCSP.CRE mice marked all airway epithelial cells including club and ciliated cells, in GFP;SFTPC.CRE mice most airway and all alveolar epithelial type II cells, and in GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice some alveolar epithelial type II cells and all alveolar macrophages (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplements 6–8, Figure 1—figure supplement 7—source data 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 8—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplements 6–8.

claim: GFP;CCSP.CRE mice show precise airway epithelial lineage labeling.
source: These findings show precise airway epithelial lineage labeling in GFP;CCSP.CRE mice and non-specific airway/alveolar/myeloid lineage labeling in GFP;SFTPC.CRE and GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice.
evidence: Based on inference from the co-localization data presented in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplements 6–8.

claim: GFP;SFTPC.CRE and GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice show non-specific airway/alveolar/myeloid lineage labeling.
source: These findings show precise airway epithelial lineage labeling in GFP;CCSP.CRE mice and non-specific airway/alveolar/myeloid lineage labeling in GFP;SFTPC.CRE and GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice.
evidence: Based on inference from the co-localization data presented in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplements 6–8.

claim: Preneoplastic and neoplastic lesions were located both in the airways and the alveolar regions in urethane and MCA/BHT models.
source: In both models, preneoplastic (airway epithelial hyperplasias and atypical alveolar hyperplasias) and neoplastic (adenoma and LUAD) lesions classified according to established guidelines (Nikitin et al., 2004) were located both in the airways and the alveolar regions.
evidence: Supported by data from experiments using urethane and MCA/BHT models, with reference to classification guidelines (Nikitin et al., 2004).

claim: Established lung tumors were most frequently located near or inside the airways.
source: However, established lung tumors were most frequently located near or inside the airways (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 11).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 11.

claim: All hyperplasias and tumors of GFP;CCSP.CRE mice contained GFP-labeled airway cells that did not express CCSP anymore, but had acquired expression of SFTPC with or without LYZ2.
source: Interestingly, all hyperplasias and tumors of GFP;CCSP.CRE mice contained GFP-labeled airway cells that did not express the club cell marker CCSP anymore, but had acquired expression of the alveolar epithelial markers SFTPC with or without LYZ2 (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplements 12–15, and Figure 1—figure supplement 13—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplements 12–15.

claim: Single urethane hits to GFP;CCSP.CRE, GFP;SFTPC.CRE, and GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice backcrossed >F12 to the susceptible FVB strain result in human LUAD-like mutations including KrasQ61R.
source: Identical results were recapitulated using single urethane hits to GFP;CCSP.CRE, GFP;SFTPC.CRE, and GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice backcrossed >F12 to the susceptible FVB strain, which result in human LUAD-like mutations including KrasQ61R (Westcott et al., 2015; Vreka et al., 2018; Kanellakis et al., 2019) (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplements 16–19).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplements 16–19, and citations to published literature (Westcott et al., 2015; Vreka et al., 2018; Kanellakis et al., 2019).

claim: Airway cells contribute to chemical-induced LUAD, shifting from airway to alveolar marker expression during carcinogenesis.
source: Collectively, these data support that airway cells contribute to chemical-induced LUAD, shifting from airway to alveolar marker expression during carcinogenesis.
evidence: Based on inference from the data presented in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplements 12–19.

claim: GFP-labeled cells of both GFP;CCSP.CRE and GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice had KrasQ61R mutations at one week post-urethane.
source: Interestingly, GFP-labeled cells of both mouse strains had KrasQ61R mutations at one week post-urethane, but KrasQ61R mutations selectively persisted in GFP-labeled airway cells in the lungs of GFP;CCSP.CRE mice at two weeks (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: KrasQ61R mutations selectively persisted in GFP-labeled airway cells in the lungs of GFP;CCSP.CRE mice at two weeks post-urethane.
source: Interestingly, GFP-labeled cells of both mouse strains had KrasQ61R mutations at one week post-urethane, but KrasQ61R mutations selectively persisted in GFP-labeled airway cells in the lungs of GFP;CCSP.CRE mice at two weeks (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Most lung tumors were spatially linked with the airways as revealed by three-dimensional reconstruction of tumor-bearing lungs using high-resolution micro-computed tomography (μCT).
source: In addition, three-dimensional reconstruction of tumor-bearing lungs of FVB mice at 6 months post-urethane using high-resolution micro-computed tomography (μCT) revealed that most lung tumors were spatially linked with the airways, in accord with pathology results (Figure 2B and C, and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by μCT data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Airway cells are involved in chemical-induced lung adenocarcinoma formation in mice.
source: These results support the involvement of airway cells in chemical-induced lung adenocarcinoma formation in mice.
evidence: Based on inference from the data presented in Figure 2A-C showing KrasQ61R mutations persisting in airway cells and spatial linkage of tumors with airways.

claim: Markedly increased numbers of GFP-labeled cells were found in the alveoli of carcinogen-treated GFP;CCSP.CRE mice compared with saline-treated or naïve controls.
source: Since airborne carcinogens act globally on the respiratory field (Franklin et al., 1997), we examined non-neoplastic alveolar areas of carcinogen-treated GFP;CCSP.CRE mice, to discover markedly increased numbers of GFP-labeled cells in the alveoli of carcinogen-treated mice compared with saline-treated or naïve controls (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2, and citation to Franklin et al., 1997.

claim: Juxtabronchial GFP-labeled cells still expressed CCSP, but lost CCSP and acquired SFTPC expression when located in alveoli and tumors.
source: Immunostaining revealed that juxtabronchial GFP-labeled cells still expressed CCSP, but lost CCSP and acquired SFTPC expression when located in alveoli and tumors (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: The expansion of airway cells after urethane exposure was documented using bioluminescent imaging of double heterozygote offspring of CCSP.CRE intercrosses with Luciferase-expressing (LUC) mice.
source: The expansion of airway cells after urethane exposure was also documented using bioluminescent imaging of double heterozygote offspring of CCSP.CRE intercrosses with Luciferase-expressing (LUC) mice (Safran et al., 2003), a strain emitting light specifically from airway epithelia (Figure 3—figure supplement 5, and Figure 3—figure supplement 5—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescent imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5, and citation to Safran et al., 2003.

claim: Co-staining of human LUAD for SFTPC and the airway markers CCSP and KRT5 showed co-localization of SFTPC with KRT5 but not with CCSP.
source: In addition, co-staining of human LUAD (Giopanou et al., 2015) for the alveolar marker SFTPC and the airway markers CCSP and KRT5 showed co-localization of SFTPC with KRT5 but not with CCSP (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 6, and citation to Giopanou et al., 2015.

claim: Airway epithelial cells expand to alveolar regions during field cancerization by tobacco carcinogens.
source: These results suggest that airway epithelial cells expand to alveolar regions during field cancerization by tobacco carcinogens, a process involving either direct alveolar cell recycling by airway epithelial cells or transient CCSP expression by alveolar cells during carcinogenesis.
evidence: Based on inference from the data presented in Figure 3A-C showing increased GFP-labeled cells in alveoli and marker expression changes.

claim: Human and murine LUAD carry airway imprints although their location and protein expression suggests an alveolar origin.
source: Moreover, that human and murine LUAD carry airway imprints although their location and protein expression suggests an alveolar origin (Desai et al., 2014; Aberle et al., 2011; Mason et al., 2000; Lindskog et al., 2014; Sutherland and Berns, 2010).
evidence: Based on inference from the data presented in Figure 3C showing co-localization of SFTPC with KRT5 in human LUAD, and citations to published literature (Desai et al., 2014; Aberle et al., 2011; Mason et al., 2000; Lindskog et al., 2014; Sutherland and Berns, 2010).

claim: The number of GFP-labeled cells in the alveoli of aging GFP;CCSP.CRE mice progressively increased and expressed SFTPC protein.
source: While the number of GFP-labeled cells in the alveoli of aging GFP;SFTPC.CRE and GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice was stable, GFP-labeled airway cells in the alveoli of aging GFP;CCSP.CRE mice progressively increased and expressed SFTPC protein (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The number of GFP-labeled cells in the alveoli of aging GFP;SFTPC.CRE and GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice was stable.
source: While the number of GFP-labeled cells in the alveoli of aging GFP;SFTPC.CRE and GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice was stable, GFP-labeled airway cells in the alveoli of aging GFP;CCSP.CRE mice progressively increased and expressed SFTPC protein (Figure 4A and B and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Bleomycin treatment accelerated the accumulation of GFP-labeled airway cells in the alveoli and in urethane-triggered LUAD.
source: Bleomycin treatment, which depletes alveolar type II cells (Lawson et al., 2005), accelerated the accumulation of GFP-labeled airway cells in the alveoli and in urethane-triggered LUAD (Figure 4C and D, Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2, Figure 4—source data 2, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4C and D, Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2, and citation to Lawson et al., 2005.

claim: GFP-labeled airway cells expressing the alveolar marker SFTPC increased in the alveoli of GFP;CCSP.CRE mice exposed to perinatal hyperoxia.
source: GFP-labeled airway cells expressing the alveolar marker SFTPC also increased in the alveoli of GFP;CCSP.CRE mice exposed to perinatal hyperoxia that damages forming alveoli (Rawlins et al., 2009), and in the alveoli of GFP;CCSP.CRE mice treated with naphthalene that kills airway epithelial cells (Sutherland and Berns, 2010; Rawlins et al., 2009), but were not identified within the airways of naphthalene-treated GFP;CCSP.CRE mice; these appeared to be repopulated by GFP-labeled airway cells that express the club cell marker CCSP (Figure 4E–4H, Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4, Figure 4—source datas 3 and 4, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E–4H and Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4, and citations to Rawlins et al., 2009 and Sutherland and Berns, 2010.

claim: GFP-labeled airway cells expressing the alveolar marker SFTPC increased in the alveoli of GFP;CCSP.CRE mice treated with naphthalene.
source: GFP-labeled airway cells expressing the alveolar marker SFTPC also increased in the alveoli of GFP;CCSP.CRE mice exposed to perinatal hyperoxia that damages forming alveoli (Rawlins et al., 2009), and in the alveoli of GFP;CCSP.CRE mice treated with naphthalene that kills airway epithelial cells (Sutherland and Berns, 2010; Rawlins et al., 2009), but were not identified within the airways of naphthalene-treated GFP;CCSP.CRE mice; these appeared to be repopulated by GFP-labeled airway cells that express the club cell marker CCSP (Figure 4E–4H, Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4, Figure 4—source datas 3 and 4, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E–4H and Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4, and citations to Rawlins et al., 2009 and Sutherland and Berns, 2010.

claim: Airways of naphthalene-treated GFP;CCSP.CRE mice appeared to be repopulated by GFP-labeled airway cells that express the club cell marker CCSP.
source: GFP-labeled airway cells expressing the alveolar marker SFTPC also increased in the alveoli of GFP;CCSP.CRE mice exposed to perinatal hyperoxia that damages forming alveoli (Rawlins et al., 2009), and in the alveoli of GFP;CCSP.CRE mice treated with naphthalene that kills airway epithelial cells (Sutherland and Berns, 2010; Rawlins et al., 2009), but were not identified within the airways of naphthalene-treated GFP;CCSP.CRE mice; these appeared to be repopulated by GFP-labeled airway cells that express the club cell marker CCSP (Figure 4E–4H, Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4, Figure 4—source datas 3 and 4, and Figure 4—figure supplement 4—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4E–4H and Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: No GFP-labeled alveolar cells were identified in the airways of GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice recovering from naphthalene-induced injury.
source: In line with the latter finding, no GFP-labeled alveolar cells were identified in the airways of GFP;LYZ2.CRE mice recovering from naphthalene-induced injury (Figure 4G and H).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claim: Airway-originated cells repopulate both the airways and the alveoli during aging and recovery from injury.
source: Taken together, the data indicate that airway-originated cells repopulate both the airways and the alveoli during aging and recovery from injury, while alveolar cells do not reconstitute the airways, in line with previous findings (Desai et al., 2014; Rawlins et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on inference from the data presented in Figure 4A-H, and citations to published literature (Desai et al., 2014; Rawlins et al., 2009).

claim: Alveolar cells do not reconstitute the airways.
source: Taken together, the data indicate that airway-originated cells repopulate both the airways and the alveoli during aging and recovery from injury, while alveolar cells do not reconstitute the airways, in line with previous findings (Desai et al., 2014; Rawlins et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on inference from the data presented in Figure 4A-H, and citations to published literature (Desai et al., 2014; Rawlins et al., 2009).

claim: SFTPC.CRE;DTA and GFP;SFTPC.CRE;DTA mice were fetal lethal.
source: As expected, SFTPC.CRE;DTA and GFP;SFTPC.CRE;DTA mice were fetal lethal (no double or triple heterozygote offspring was obtained by n > 3 intercrosses,>10 litters, and >60 off-springs for each genotype; p<0.0001, Fischer's exact test).
evidence: Supported by data from breeding experiments showing no double or triple heterozygote offspring (n > 3 intercrosses, >10 litters, and >60 off-springs for each genotype; p<0.0001, Fischer's exact test).

claim: Airway epithelial ablation was complete in GFP;CCSP.CRE;DTA mice.
source: Airway epithelial ablation was complete in GFP;CCSP.CRE;DTA mice, while some GFP-labeled alveolar macrophages persisted in GFP;LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice, presumably freshly recruited monocytes initiating LYZ2 expression.
evidence: Supported by data from ablation experiments in GFP;CCSP.CRE;DTA mice.

claim: Some GFP-labeled alveolar macrophages persisted in GFP;LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice, presumably freshly recruited monocytes initiating LYZ2 expression.
source: Airway epithelial ablation was complete in GFP;CCSP.CRE;DTA mice, while some GFP-labeled alveolar macrophages persisted in GFP;LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice, presumably freshly recruited monocytes initiating LYZ2 expression.
evidence: Supported by data from ablation experiments in GFP;LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice, with speculation about the origin of persisting cells.

claim: The denuded airway epithelium of 12-week-old GFP;CCSP.CRE;DTA mice contained few flat CCSP+SFTPC+LYZ2+ immunoreactive cells.
source: Immunostaining revealed that the denuded airway epithelium of 12-week-old GFP;CCSP.CRE;DTA mice contained few flat CCSP+SFTPC+LYZ2+ immunoreactive cells, while the apparently intact alveolar spaces of GFP;LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice harbored only some CCSP-SFTPC-LYZ2+immunoreactive alveolar macrophages (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The apparently intact alveolar spaces of GFP;LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice harbored only some CCSP-SFTPC-LYZ2+ immunoreactive alveolar macrophages.
source: Immunostaining revealed that the denuded airway epithelium of 12-week-old GFP;CCSP.CRE;DTA mice contained few flat CCSP+SFTPC+LYZ2+ immunoreactive cells, while the apparently intact alveolar spaces of GFP;LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice harbored only some CCSP-SFTPC-LYZ2+immunoreactive alveolar macrophages (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice displayed normal airway caliper and mean linear intercept compared with DTA controls.
source: Remarkably, morphometric and functional analyses of 12-week-old DTA control, CCSP.CRE;DTA, and LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice showed that LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice displayed normal airway caliper and mean linear intercept (measures of airway and alveolar structure), normal number of CD45+ CD11b+ myeloid cells in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL; measure of airspace inflammation), and normal airways resistance and static compliance (measures of airway and alveolar function) compared with DTA controls.
evidence: Supported by morphometric and functional data from 12-week-old DTA control, CCSP.CRE;DTA, and LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice.

claim: LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice displayed normal number of CD45+ CD11b+ myeloid cells in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) compared with DTA controls.
source: Remarkably, morphometric and functional analyses of 12-week-old DTA control, CCSP.CRE;DTA, and LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice showed that LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice displayed normal airway caliper and mean linear intercept (measures of airway and alveolar structure), normal number of CD45+ CD11b+ myeloid cells in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL; measure of airspace inflammation), and normal airways resistance and static compliance (measures of airway and alveolar function) compared with DTA controls.
evidence: Supported by morphometric and functional data from 12-week-old DTA control, CCSP.CRE;DTA, and LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice.

claim: LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice displayed normal airways resistance and static compliance compared with DTA controls.
source: Remarkably, morphometric and functional analyses of 12-week-old DTA control, CCSP.CRE;DTA, and LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice showed that LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice displayed normal airway caliper and mean linear intercept (measures of airway and alveolar structure), normal number of CD45+ CD11b+ myeloid cells in bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL; measure of airspace inflammation), and normal airways resistance and static compliance (measures of airway and alveolar function) compared with DTA controls.
evidence: Supported by morphometric and functional data from 12-week-old DTA control, CCSP.CRE;DTA, and LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice.

claim: CCSP.CRE;DTA mice displayed widened airway and alveolar dimensions with inflammatory interalveolar septal destruction evident by increased mean linear intercept, CD45+ CD11b+ cells in BAL, and static compliance.
source: However, CCSP.CRE;DTA mice displayed widened airway and alveolar dimensions with inflammatory interalveolar septal destruction evident by increased mean linear intercept, CD45+ CD11b+ cells in BAL, and static compliance (Figure 5B and C and Figure 5—source data 1), mimicking human chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (Barnes et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by morphometric and functional data shown in Figure 5B and C, and citation to Barnes et al., 2015.

claim: CCSP.CRE;DTA mice mimic human chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
source: However, CCSP.CRE;DTA mice displayed widened airway and alveolar dimensions with inflammatory interalveolar septal destruction evident by increased mean linear intercept, CD45+ CD11b+ cells in BAL, and static compliance (Figure 5B and C and Figure 5—source data 1), mimicking human chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (Barnes et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on inference from the morphometric and functional data shown in Figure 5B and C, and citation to Barnes et al., 2015.

claim: CCSP.CRE;DTA and LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice were equally protected from LUAD development compared with controls.
source: Finally, we exposed control and ablated mice to ten consecutive weekly urethane exposures. All mice survived six months into carcinogen treatment, and CCSP.CRE;DTA and LYZ2.CRE;DTA mice were equally protected from LUAD development compared with controls (Figure 5D and E, and Figure 5—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5D and E from urethane exposure experiments.

claim: The CCSP+ airway lineage maintains postnatal alveolar structure and function.
source: Taken together, these results show that the CCSP+ airway lineage maintains postnatal alveolar structure and function, and, together with the LYZ2+ alveolar lineage, are required for lung adenocarcinoma development.
evidence: Based on inference from the data presented in Figure 5A-E showing effects of airway cell ablation on alveolar structure and function.

claim: The CCSP+ airway lineage and the LYZ2+ alveolar lineage are required for lung adenocarcinoma development.
source: Taken together, these results show that the CCSP+ airway lineage maintains postnatal alveolar structure and function, and, together with the LYZ2+ alveolar lineage, are required for lung adenocarcinoma development.
evidence: Based on inference from the data presented in Figure 5D and E showing protection from LUAD in ablated mice.

claim: The AEC transcriptome was specifically enriched in LUAD cells compared with whole lungs.
source: The AEC transcriptome was specifically enriched in LUAD cells compared with whole lungs (Figure 6A and B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1, and Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 6A and B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: LUAD cell lines lost expression of epithelial markers compared with their native lungs.
source: LUAD cell lines lost expression of epithelial markers compared with their native lungs, but displayed up-regulated expression of LUAD markers (i.e., Krt18 and Krt20), of epidermal growth factor receptor ligands (Areg and Ereg), and of the Myc oncogene (Figure 6—figure supplements 2–4, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 2–4.

claim: LUAD cell lines displayed up-regulated expression of LUAD markers (i.e., Krt18 and Krt20), of epidermal growth factor receptor ligands (Areg and Ereg), and of the Myc oncogene.
source: LUAD cell lines lost expression of epithelial markers compared with their native lungs, but displayed up-regulated expression of LUAD markers (i.e., Krt18 and Krt20), of epidermal growth factor receptor ligands (Areg and Ereg), and of the Myc oncogene (Figure 6—figure supplements 2–4, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 2–4.

claim: The AEC transcriptome was significantly enriched in human LUAD compared with healthy lungs.
source: Similar analyses of the transcriptomes of human LUAD and corresponding healthy lungs (Kabbout et al., 2013), and of primary human AEC, ATII, and AMΦ (Clark et al., 2015; Dancer et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2009) also disclosed that the AEC transcriptome was significantly enriched in LUAD compared with healthy lungs (Figure 6C and D and Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: Supported by microarray data shown in Figure 6C and D, and citations to published literature (Kabbout et al., 2013; Clark et al., 2015; Dancer et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2009).

claim: The mouse AEC transcriptome predominated over ATII/BMDM transcriptomes in LUAD cells.
source: Gene set enrichment analyses (GSEA) showed that the mouse AEC transcriptome predominated over ATII/BMDM transcriptomes in LUAD cells (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 5, and Figure 6—source data 3).
evidence: Supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: The human AEC transcriptome was enriched equally with ATII/AMΦ transcriptomes in human LUAD compared with healthy lungs.
source: In addition, the human AEC transcriptome was enriched equally with ATII/AMΦ transcriptomes in human LUAD compared with healthy lungs (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 6, and Figure 6—source data 4).
evidence: Supported by GSEA data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 6.

claim: There is a presence of an anticipated alveolar and an unexpected airway epithelial transcriptomic signature in tobacco carcinogen-induced LUAD of mice and men.
source: These results showed the presence of an anticipated alveolar and an unexpected airway epithelial transcriptomic signature in tobacco carcinogen-induced LUAD of mice and men.
evidence: Based on inference from the GSEA data presented in Figure 6E and F.

claim: Club cells survive KRAS mutations and form lung tumors after tobacco carcinogen exposure.
source: Club cells are shown to survive KRAS mutations and to form lung tumors after tobacco carcinogen exposure.
evidence: Supported by data from ddPCR experiments (Figure 2A) and lineage tracing experiments (Figure 1D) showing KrasQ61R mutations persisting in airway cells and GFP-labeled tumors in GFP;CCSP.CRE mice.

claim: Increasing numbers of club cells are found in the alveoli with aging and after lung injury.
source: Increasing numbers of club cells are found in the alveoli with aging and after lung injury, but go undetected since they express alveolar proteins.
evidence: Supported by data from aging and injury experiments (Figure 4A-H) showing increased GFP-labeled cells in alveoli expressing SFTPC.

claim: Club cells in the alveoli go undetected since they express alveolar proteins.
source: Increasing numbers of club cells are found in the alveoli with aging and after lung injury, but go undetected since they express alveolar proteins.
evidence: Supported by data from immunostaining experiments (Figure 3B, Figure 4A) showing GFP-labeled airway cells expressing SFTPC in alveoli.

claim: Ablation of club cells prevents chemical lung tumors.
source: Ablation of club cells prevents chemical lung tumors and causes alveolar destruction in adult mice.
evidence: Supported by data from ablation experiments (Figure 5D and E) showing protection from LUAD in CCSP.CRE;DTA mice.

claim: Ablation of club cells causes alveolar destruction in adult mice.
source: Ablation of club cells prevents chemical lung tumors and causes alveolar destruction in adult mice.
evidence: Supported by data from ablation experiments (Figure 5B and C) showing increased mean linear intercept and inflammatory destruction in CCSP.CRE;DTA mice.

claim: Club cells are important in alveolar maintenance and carcinogenesis.
source: Hence club cells are important in alveolar maintenance and carcinogenesis and may be a therapeutic target against premalignancy and chronic lung disease.
evidence: Based on inference from the data presented throughout the manuscript showing club cell involvement in alveolar maintenance (Figure 4, Figure 5) and carcinogenesis (Figure 1, Figure 2).

claim: Club cells may be a therapeutic target against premalignancy and chronic lung disease.
source: Hence club cells are important in alveolar maintenance and carcinogenesis and may be a therapeutic target against premalignancy and chronic lung disease.
evidence: Based on speculation from the findings showing club cell involvement in alveolar maintenance and carcinogenesis.
